items.title: A bottle with no inside
items.claim: A normal bottle has an inside and an outside, separated by the bottle wall. The Klein bottle has no inside. There is only one surface — what looks like 'inside' is connected to 'outside' through the surface itself.
items.prompt: How is the Klein bottle different from a regular surface?

options.text: It's non-orientable — there is no consistent way to assign 'outward normals'; a left-handed walker traversing it can come back as right-handed
It's actually two surfaces glued together
Klein bottles only exist in imagination

items.reveal:
Klein constructed the bottle as a 2D analogue of the Möbius strip — but closed. To build one in 3D, you must let the bottle 'pass through itself' (a fake self-intersection). Properly, it lives in 4-dimensional space, where it has no intersection.

In rigorous terms: the Klein bottle is a non-orientable, closed 2-manifold with Euler characteristic 0. It cannot be embedded in 3D Euclidean space without self-intersection.

The Möbius strip (Möbius, 1858) is a 2D example with boundary: cut one open and you get a long strip; cut it in half lengthwise and you get a single longer Möbius strip, not two.

Non-orientable surfaces matter in physics (some condensed matter systems behave like Möbius strips), engineering (conveyor belt design uses Möbius topology to wear evenly), and cosmology (toy models of non-orientable universes have been considered, though our universe seems to be orientable).
items.why: 3D objects have an obvious inside and outside. Topology shows some 2D surfaces don't — the apparently obvious 'inside/outside' distinction is a special feature of orientable manifolds.

items.title: Matrices don't commute — and that's why quantum mechanics works
items.claim: AB is not generally equal to BA for matrices. The order of operations matters. This isn't a defect — it's the most important feature of matrix algebra and the mathematical foundation of quantum uncertainty.

options.text: Matrices represent linear transformations of vectors; applying transformation A then B is generally not the same as B then A. The non-commutativity reflects that composition of transformations in higher dimensions does NOT commute in general
AB = BA always works for invertible matrices

items.reveal:
For matrices, AB and BA are generally different — and AB is well-defined only when A's columns equal B's rows. Even for square matrices of the same size, AB and BA can differ wildly.

Example: A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]], B = [[1, 0], [1, 1]].
AB = [[2, 1], [1, 1]].
BA = [[1, 1], [1, 2]]. Different.

When does AB = BA? Some special cases: scalar multiples of identity; same diagonal matrix; simultaneously diagonalisable matrices; powers of the same matrix.

The commutator [A, B] = AB - BA measures the non-commutativity. For ordinary numbers it's always zero; for matrices it can be anything.

In QUANTUM MECHANICS:
- Physical observables are represented as matrices (or operators on Hilbert space).
- The commutator of position and momentum: [x, p] = i * hbar. Non-zero!
- Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: the variance of two non-commuting observables, in any state, has a lower bound proportional to the commutator. You can't simultaneously know position and momentum precisely.

This is not a measurement limitation — it's a structural feature of the math. Eigenvectors of non-commuting matrices are different; states have to choose between definite x and definite p.

Lie groups and algebras: continuous symmetry transformations form groups whose generators are matrices with commutation relations. The group SU(3) underlies the strong nuclear force; SU(2) describes weak force and quantum spin; U(1) describes electromagnetism. The standard model of particle physics is built from non-commuting matrices.

In computer graphics: rotation matrices in 3D don't commute (mentioned in another card). The order matters when composing transformations.
items.why: Multiplication seems naturally commutative. For matrices it isn't — and the depth of this fact is that quantum mechanics, particle physics, computer graphics, and most of modern physics rely on it.

items.title: 20% of people own 80% of the wealth — and 4% own 64%
items.claim: Vilfredo Pareto observed in 1896 that ~20% of Italians owned ~80% of the land. The pattern recurs in income, book sales, software bugs, city sizes, earthquake magnitudes. Apply 80/20 again to that 20%: 4% own 64%. And again: 0.8% own 51.2%.
items.prompt: Why is this 'fractal' inequality so common?

options.text: Many natural and social processes follow POWER LAWS: P(X > x) is proportional to x to some negative power. Power-law distributions exhibit self-similarity at all scales, including the recursive 80/20 split
It is true only for exactly 20%

items.reveal:
A power-law distribution: the probability that a quantity exceeds x is proportional to x^(-alpha), for some exponent alpha. The Pareto distribution is the canonical example.

When alpha is in a particular range (specifically when the exponent gives an 80/20 split), the distribution is 'self-similar': the top 20% has 80% of the total; within that top 20%, the top 20% (i.e., the top 4%) holds 80% of THEIR share (i.e., 64% of the whole).

Key examples:
- US household wealth: top 20% own ~85%; top 1% own ~32%.
- Earthquakes: each unit increase in magnitude is ~10x less frequent.
- City sizes (Zipf's law, also power law).
- Web site visits, book sales, file sizes, software bug counts.
- Word frequencies in language (Zipf).

Generative mechanisms: 'rich-get-richer' (preferential attachment, scale-free networks — Barabási, Albert 1999); multiplicative growth; minimax processes.

Power laws contrast with normal distributions (bell curves) where extreme values are vanishingly rare. In power-law distributions, extreme values dominate — and you can't reason about averages as 'typical'.
items.why: Equality intuitions assume bell curves. Many real distributions are power laws — where the top few items dwarf the rest, and inequality is built into the math.
